summary.text: The mesosphere is the third layer of Earth's atmosphere, sitting directly above the stratosphere and directly below the thermosphere.
Its average temperature drops with height, and its top, the mesopause, is the coldest part of Earth's atmosphere at below −143 °C.
It lies above aircraft altitude records but below where spacecraft can orbit, so only sounding rockets have reached it, leaving it the least-understood part of the atmosphere.

facts.value: Usually 47 to 51 km above sea level

facts.label: Sodium layer
facts.value: 5 km deep, between 80 and 105 km up

items.prompt: A research team wants direct measurements from the middle of the mesosphere. What is their realistic way to get instruments there?

options.label: Launch a sounding rocket for a few minutes
Send up a large high-altitude balloon
Park a satellite in a low orbit there
Fly a high-altitude research jet up to it

items.explain: The layer is above aircraft records, mostly above balloon reach, and too draggy for orbiting craft, so only sounding rockets get there, for minutes at a time.

items.prompt: Scientists jokingly call the mesosphere the 'ignorosphere'. What earned it that name?

options.label: Sunlight passes through it without heating it
It is so hard to reach that it is poorly studied
It has no effect on the layers around it
Radio signals pass straight through it

items.explain: Planes and most balloons cannot reach it and satellites cannot orbit in it, so it is the least-understood part of the atmosphere.

items.prompt: Imagine rising from the bottom to the top of the mesosphere. What happens to the average temperature on the way up?

options.label: It climbs steadily higher
It stays about the same
It keeps dropping, coldest at the top
It rises first, then evens out

items.explain: The average temperature falls with altitude, and the top of the layer, the mesopause, is the coldest place in Earth's atmosphere.

items.prompt: The mesosphere holds a thin band of sodium atoms that keeps getting topped up. Where does that sodium come from?

options.label: Sea spray lifted by storms
Gases from erupting volcanoes
Particles streaming from the Sun
Incoming meteors burning away

items.explain: The band is regularly replenished by sodium sublimating from incoming meteors.

items.prompt: Astronomers on the ground make use of the mesosphere's sodium band. What do they use it for?

options.label: Making artificial guide stars for sharper images
Measuring how far away the Moon is
Blocking city light from their telescopes
Timing the arrival of solar storms

items.explain: The sodium band is used to create 'guide stars' for the optical correction that produces ultra-sharp ground-based observations.

items.prompt: Why can't a satellite simply circle Earth at mesosphere altitudes?

options.label: Its electronics would freeze solid
The air there would slow it too much
Earth's gravity is too strong there
Constant lightning would destroy it

items.explain: The mesosphere is below the minimum altitude for orbiting spacecraft because of high atmospheric drag.

paragraphs.heading: Where it sits
paragraphs.text: The mesosphere is the third layer of air above Earth, resting directly on the stratosphere with the thermosphere directly above it. Its name comes from the Ancient Greek word for middle. Its bottom edge usually lies 47 to 51 km above sea level and its top usually between 85 and 100 km, though both shift with latitude and season. Together with the stratosphere, it is sometimes called the middle atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Colder with height
paragraphs.text: Climb through the mesosphere and the air keeps getting colder. One reason is that the thin air holds a shrinking share of ozone higher up, so it absorbs less sunlight; ozone is the main absorber of the ultraviolet light that gets past the thermosphere. Another reason is that carbon dioxide (CO₂) sheds more and more heat by radiating it away. Its top, the mesopause, is the coldest spot in the whole atmosphere of Earth, below −143 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Waves and winds
paragraphs.text: This region is shaped by strong east-west winds, atmospheric tides, gravity waves and planetary waves. Most of these tides and waves begin lower down, in the troposphere and lower stratosphere, and travel upward. In the mesosphere, gravity waves can grow so large that they turn unstable and break apart. When that happens they hand their momentum to the mesosphere, and this largely drives the circulation of the whole atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Metals from meteors
paragraphs.text: Millions of meteors enter the atmosphere, averaging 40,000 tons a year. Sodium that sublimates from them keeps topping up a band of sodium atoms about 5 km deep, sitting between 80 and 105 km up. These atoms are neither bound nor ionized, and they glow weakly, adding to the airglow. Astronomers have begun using this band to make artificial guide stars, part of a correction process that lets telescopes on the ground produce ultra-sharp observations. Layers of other metals, such as iron and potassium, also exist near the top of the mesosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Night clouds and new auroras
paragraphs.text: Noctilucent clouds form in the mesosphere, and the smoke left by burning-up meteors is thought to act as the seeds they condense around. Since October 2018, scientists have identified a distinct kind of aurora that starts in this layer, about 96 km up. Nicknamed dunes, its green, rippling lights look like ripples of sand on a beach and stretch toward the equator. The green color has tentatively been explained by fast solar particles striking oxygen molecules.

paragraphs.heading: The ignorosphere
paragraphs.text: The mesosphere is very hard to reach. It lies above the altitude records for aircraft, balloons can get only into its lowest few kilometres, and air drag is too high for spacecraft to orbit there. Only sounding rockets have reached it, and each one can take measurements for just a few minutes. So it remains the least-understood layer of the atmosphere, earning the joking nickname ignorosphere.
